prompt: Why are metal carbonyls often used as starting materials for making other coordination compounds?

choices.text: CO has no charge and is a gas, so a substitution can be driven to the right by purging CO out of the vessel
CO is the strongest σ-donor known, so it is easy to replace with weaker donors
choices.why: The section doesn't call CO the strongest σ-donor; cyanide, for one, is a stronger σ-donor. The useful features are that CO is neutral and a gas.

choices.text: CO stabilizes metals in high oxidation states, which are easy to substitute
choices.why: It is the reverse: CO's π-accepting properties stabilize metals in low, even negative, oxidation states.

choices.text: CO always bridges two metals, so it falls off easily
choices.why: CO is often a terminal ligand bound to one metal. Bridging isn't why carbonyls make good starting materials.

explanation: Carbonyls are frequently used as starting materials for other coordination compounds because the carbonyl ligand has no charge and carbon monoxide is a gas. A ligand substitution reaction can therefore be driven to the right by purging CO out of the reaction vessel.

prompt: CO binds to metals through carbon rather than oxygen, even though oxygen is more electronegative. Why?

choices.text: CO's HOMO is a roughly nonbonding orbital located mainly on carbon, the carbon lone pair
Carbon is the more electronegative atom, so its lone pair is held more strongly
choices.why: Carbon is the less electronegative atom; that is exactly why its preference is not obvious.

choices.text: The oxygen lone pair is the HOMO, but it is blocked from the metal by steric hindrance
choices.why: The oxygen lone pair is in the 2a1 orbital, which lies significantly lower in energy than the HOMO, so it is rarely used in bonding.

choices.text: CO's π* orbital is localized mainly on oxygen, so oxygen can't bond to the metal
choices.why: The π* orbital is mostly localized on carbon, the more electropositive atom.

explanation: The carbon end of CO is the more reactive end because the HOMO is an approximately nonbonding orbital localized mainly on carbon, the carbon lone pair in the valence bond picture. The oxygen lone pair corresponds to the 2a1 orbital, which is much lower in energy and rarely used. The π and π* orbitals are close enough in energy to the HOMO to also take part in bonding.

prompt: What is a semibridging carbonyl ligand?

choices.text: A CO bridging two different metals joined by a metal–metal bond, interacting more strongly with one of them
A CO that donates through both its carbon and oxygen lone pairs
choices.why: That is an isocarbonyl ligand, a rare 4-electron donor mode.

choices.text: A CO whose carbon lone pair is shared among three metals
choices.why: That is a μ3-bridging carbonyl.

choices.text: A CO bound side-on to a single metal through its π* orbital
choices.why: That is one of the π-binding modes of CO, not a σ-bridging mode.

explanation: When the two metals held together by a metal–metal bond are different, CO's interaction with one metal may be stronger than with the other, and the CO is called semibridging. In the terminal, μ-bridged, μ3-bridged and semibridging modes alike, CO is a 2-electron donor, donating its carbon lone pair.

prompt: A CO ligand bridges three metals in a μ3-η^2 mode: its carbon lone pair binds one metal, and its four bonding π electrons are shared with the other two metals, one π pair each. How many electrons does this CO donate?
explanation: The carbon lone pair gives 2 electrons and the two π pairs give 2 + 2, so the CO is a 6-electron donor. Compare the μ2-η^2 mode (lone pair to one metal, one π pair to another), a 4-electron donor, and the other μ3-η^2 mode in which the lone pair is shared by two metals and one π pair goes to the third, also a 4-electron donor.

prompt: In the Dewar–Chatt–Duncanson model, how does σ donation from CO reinforce π back-donation to CO?

choices.text: The donated density raises the energy of the metal d electrons through electron–electron repulsion, so CO accepts them more easily into π*
The donated density lowers the energy of the metal d electrons, so they sit closer in energy to CO π*
choices.why: σ donation raises the d-electron energies through increased repulsion. That rise is what makes back-donation easier.

choices.text: σ donation empties the metal d orbitals so that CO can donate its π electrons into them
choices.why: The donated lone pair goes into empty metal d orbitals, and back-donation moves metal d electrons into CO's empty π* orbitals.

choices.text: σ donation raises the C–O bond order, and a stronger C–O bond accepts π electrons better
choices.why: In this model the C–O bond order goes down, because back-donation puts electron density into CO's π* orbitals.

explanation: The carbon lone pair donates electron density into empty metal d orbitals, forming a dative bond. This raises the energy of the metal d electrons through increased electron–electron repulsion, so they are more easily accepted by CO's π* orbitals. Back-donation then increases the M–C bond order and decreases the C–O bond order, and the two interactions reinforce each other.

prompt: Which carbonyl is best drawn with an M–C triple bond and a C–O single bond, the picture for strong π-acceptor interactions?

choices.text: Cr(CO)6
choices.why: Neutral carbonyls have intermediate π-acceptor interactions, drawn with M–C and C–O double bonds.
A 1− charge still gives intermediate π-acceptor interactions. Strong interactions need a charge of 2− or more.
Carbonyl cations with a charge of +2 or higher have weak π-acceptor interactions, drawn with an M–C single bond and a C–O triple bond.

explanation: The strength of the π-acceptor interactions depends mostly on the carbonyl's charge. Charges of +2 or higher give weak interactions (M–C single, C–O triple); neutral, +1 or −1 carbonyls give intermediate ones (both double); 2− or more gives strong ones (M–C triple, C–O single). So [Fe(CO)4]^2− has the strongest M–C bond of these, and carbonylate anions are more stable than carbonyl cations.

prompt: Which of these 18-electron octahedral carbonyls has the highest C–O stretching wavenumber?

choices.why: Moving left in the period, toward vanadium, the wavenumber goes down. This anion has the lowest C–O bond order and the highest M–C bond order of the set.

choices.text: Cr(CO)6
choices.why: Chromium is in group 6. The wavenumbers increase with group number across a period, so Fe in group 8 is higher.
Mn is in group 7, one group before Fe, so its C–O stretch is lower than that of the iron dication.

explanation: The C–O stretching wavenumber measures M–C bond order indirectly: the lower the wavenumber, the lower the C–O bond order and the higher the M–C bond order. Within a period, the wavenumbers increase with group number, showing decreasing M–C bond order. [Fe(CO)6]^2+, in group 8 and with the highest positive charge, has the highest wavenumber.

prompt: An 18-electron hexacarbonyl of titanium is known. With each CO as a 2-electron donor, what charge must it carry (give the sign)?
explanation: Ti is in group 4 and contributes 4 electrons; six CO ligands add 12, giving 16. Two more electrons are needed, so the charge is 2−: [Ti(CO)6]^2−. Donor pair check: CO is neutral, so the 2− charge makes Ti(−II), with 4 + 2 = 6 electrons, and 6 + 12 = 18. Its homologues [Zr(CO)6]^2− and [Hf(CO)6]^2− are also known.

prompt: Tetrahedral 18-electron carbonylates such as [Co(CO)4]^− are stable even with high negative charges. What charge must a chromium tetracarbonyl, Cr(CO)4, carry to have 18 valence electrons (give the sign)?
explanation: Cr is in group 6 and contributes 6 electrons; four CO ligands add 8, giving 14. Four more electrons are needed, so the charge is 4−: [Cr(CO)4]^4−. Donor pair check: Cr(−IV) has 6 + 4 = 10 electrons, plus 8 from CO, giving 18. The section lists [Co(CO)4]^−, [Fe(CO)4]^2−, [Mn(CO)4]^3− and [Cr(CO)4]^4− as all stable.

prompt: Ni(CO)4 is a stable 18-electron complex, but Pd(CO)4 and Pt(CO)4 are not stable. Why?

choices.text: π overlap in tetrahedral complexes is weak, and the larger Pd and Pt orbitals overlap even less with the small CO π* orbitals
Pd(CO)4 and Pt(CO)4 would have only 16 valence electrons
choices.why: Like Ni, Pd and Pt are group 10 metals: 10 + 4 × 2 = 18 electrons, the same count as Ni(CO)4.

choices.text: Pd and Pt can't exist in the 0 oxidation state
choices.why: PF3 forms stable complexes with Pd and Pt in the oxidation number 0. The problem is weak π back-donation to CO.

choices.text: A coordination number of 4 is too low for any carbonyl
choices.why: Ni(CO)4 is stable with the same coordination number. The section calls coordination number 3 too low, for group 12.

explanation: The group 10 carbonyls M(CO)4 are tetrahedral, and π-orbital overlap in tetrahedral complexes is generally weak, so the M–C bond gets less stabilization from π-acceptor interactions than in octahedral or trigonal bipyramidal carbonyls. For Pd and Pt, the larger d orbitals overlap even less effectively with the relatively small π* orbitals of CO, so the π-acceptor interactions are too weak for a stable molecule.

prompt: With each CO as a 2-electron donor, how many CO ligands would a neutral, mononuclear 18-electron homoleptic carbonyl of a group 4 metal need?
explanation: A group 4 metal has 4 valence electrons, so the ligands must supply 18 − 4 = 14 electrons: 14/2 = 7 CO ligands. A coordination number of 7 is unacceptably high for carbonyls, so no group 4 carbonyls are stable. Group 12 fails the other way: it would need only (18 − 12)/2 = 3 CO, an unacceptably low coordination number.

prompt: Cobalt has an odd number of valence electrons, so its neutral homoleptic carbonyl forms by dimerizing a 17-electron fragment. How many CO ligands in total does this dinuclear carbonyl contain?
explanation: Co is in group 9, so a 17-electron fragment needs 17 − 9 = 8 electrons from CO: 8/2 = 4 CO, a Co(CO)4 fragment. Two fragments dimerize to Co2(CO)8, with 8 CO ligands. Only the cobalt compound is realized; the Rh and Ir analogs are unstable.

prompt: V(CO)6 is a 17-electron complex, yet unlike the 17-electron fragment Mn(CO)5 it does not dimerize. Why not?

choices.text: Dimerizing would raise vanadium's coordination number to 7, which is much less favorable than 6
It already has 18 valence electrons
choices.why: Vanadium is in group 5: 5 + 6 × 2 = 17 electrons. V(CO)6 is a radical.

choices.text: Its radical electron is sterically active and blocks the metal–metal bond
choices.why: The section says the radical electron in octahedral V(CO)6 is sterically inactive.

choices.text: Vanadium has an even number of valence electrons, so it doesn't need to dimerize
choices.why: Vanadium has 5 valence electrons, an odd number. That is why V(CO)6 has 17 electrons.

explanation: The 17-electron vanadium fragment V(CO)6 doesn't dimerize because coordination number 6 is much more favorable than 7. V(CO)6 is a dark violet, octahedral radical. It can be used as an oxidant because it is easily reduced to the 18-electron [V(CO)6]^−. Nb(CO)6 and Ta(CO)6 are not known.

prompt: W(CO)6 can be made by treating WCl6 with CO under heat and pressure. What is this kind of method called?

choices.text: Reductive carbonylation
Deinsertion of CO from dimethylformamide
choices.why: That method takes the CO from an organic carbonyl compound such as DMF, as in making IrCl(CO)(PPh3)2. Here CO gas is the source.

choices.text: Direct reaction of the elemental metal with CO
choices.why: That works for nickel and iron. Here the starting material is a high-oxidation-state complex, WCl6, not the metal.

choices.text: Oxidative carbonylation
choices.why: Tungsten goes from +6 in WCl6 to 0 in W(CO)6, so the metal is reduced, not oxidized.

explanation: Reductive carbonylation is the treatment of a high-oxidation-state complex with CO, usually with significant heat and pressure, as in WCl6 + CO → W(CO)6. Bathing the metal itself in CO fails for most carbonyls but works for nickel(0) and iron(0) ones, and deinsertion from DMF is useful for mixed carbonyls in the presence of reducing ligands like phosphines.

prompt: Cyanide, CN^−, is isoelectronic with CO and also binds through carbon. How does it compare with CO as a ligand?

choices.text: It is a stronger σ-donor and a weaker π-acceptor, and it prefers metals in high oxidation states
It is a weaker σ-donor and a stronger π-acceptor, and it prefers metals in low oxidation states
choices.why: This reverses each point. The negative charge raises CN^−'s orbital energies, making it a better σ-donor and a poorer π-acceptor.

choices.text: It is a stronger σ-donor and a stronger π-acceptor, and it stabilizes negative oxidation states like CO
choices.why: CN^−'s π* orbitals are higher in energy than CO's, so it is a weaker π-acceptor and does not stabilize low oxidation states.

choices.text: It is a weaker σ-donor and a weaker π-acceptor, and it rarely bridges two metals
choices.why: CN^− is the stronger σ-donor, and it bridges two metals far more often than CO, using both of its lone pairs.

explanation: The negative charge on CN^− increases electron–electron repulsion and raises its orbital energies, so it donates more readily (a stronger σ-donor) and accepts less readily into its higher-energy π* orbitals (a weaker π-acceptor). Electrostatically, the anion interacts best with metal cations, so unlike CO it prefers metals in high, positive oxidation states.

prompt: In trans-[Co(en)2Cl(NO)]^+, the nitrosyl is bent, with an O–N–Co angle in the range of 119 to 140°. How many electrons does the NO donate, and why is it bent?

choices.text: 1 electron; the lone pair left on N is sterically active
3 electrons; the lone pair left on N is sterically active
choices.why: If NO donates 3 electrons, its N lone pair is used in bonding and is no longer sterically active, so the nitrosyl is linear.

choices.text: 2 electrons; the radical electron left on N is sterically active
choices.why: Neutral NO can't be a 2-electron donor that keeps its radical electron. The radical electron is the highest-energy electron and is always used first.

choices.text: 1 electron; the radical electron left on N is sterically active
choices.why: The radical electron is the one donated in the 1-electron mode. What stays on N is the lone pair, and that is what bends the ligand.

explanation: NO has one more electron than CO, a radical electron, and binds through N. Donating just the radical electron makes NO a 1-electron donor; the N lone pair is then sterically active and the ligand is bent (O–N–M angles of 119 to 140°), as in trans-[Co(en)2Cl(NO)]^+. Donating the lone pair as well makes NO a 3-electron donor that binds linearly, as in nitroprusside, [Fe(CN)5(NO)]^2−.

prompt: A linear nitrosyl can also be described as an ion that donates two electrons. Which ion, and why is it linear?

choices.text: NO^+, which donates its single N lone pair and has no sterically active electrons left on N
NO^−, which donates one of its two N lone pairs and keeps the other
choices.why: That is the alternative view of a bent nitrosyl. The remaining lone pair on N is sterically active and bends the ligand.

choices.text: NO^+, which donates one of its two N lone pairs and keeps the other
choices.why: NO^+ has only one lone pair at N. Once it is donated, nothing sterically active is left, which is why the ligand is linear.

choices.text: NO^−, which donates both of its N lone pairs to the metal
choices.why: In this view each ion donates only two electrons. The NO^− ion corresponds to bent nitrosyls.

explanation: In the alternative view, a bent nitrosyl is an NO^− anion (two lone pairs at N) donating two electrons, leaving one sterically active lone pair. A linear nitrosyl is an NO^+ cation, which has one lone pair at N; when it donates that pair, no sterically active electrons remain on N, so the ligand binds linearly.

prompt: Using the neutral atom method, with the bent NO as a 1-electron donor and each ethylenediamine (en) as two L-type amine donors, what is the total valence electron count of trans-[Co(en)2Cl(NO)]^+?
explanation: Neutral Co (group 9) has 9 electrons; subtract 1 for the 1+ charge. The two en ligands give 2 × 4 = 8, Cl gives 1, and the bent NO gives 1: 9 − 1 + 8 + 1 + 1 = 18. Donor pair check, treating bent NO as NO^− (a 2-electron donor): Cl^− and NO^− with a 1+ overall charge make Co(III), d^6, and 6 + 8 + 2 + 2 = 18.

prompt: Using the neutral atom method, with the linear NO as a 3-electron donor and each cyanide counted as an X-type ligand, what is the total valence electron count of nitroprusside, [Fe(CN)5(NO)]^2−?
explanation: Neutral Fe (group 8) has 8 electrons; add 2 for the 2− charge. Five X-type cyanides give 5 × 1 = 5, and the linear NO gives 3: 8 + 2 + 5 + 3 = 18. Donor pair check, treating linear NO as NO^+ (a 2-electron donor): five CN^− and NO^+ with a 2− overall charge make Fe(II), d^6, and 6 + 5 × 2 + 2 = 18.

prompt: Using the donor pair method, with each phosphine as an L-type 2-electron donor, what is the total valence electron count of Pt(PCy3)2?
explanation: Both phosphines are neutral L-type ligands, so Pt is Pt(0) with 10 electrons (group 10). Two phosphines add 2 × 2 = 4: 10 + 4 = 14. The neutral atom method gives the same, 10 + 4 = 14. Most phosphines are too big to fit more than four around one metal, so many phosphine complexes, like Pt(PCy3)2, Pd[P(t-Bu)3]2 and [Rh(PPh3)3]^+, are coordinatively unsaturated, and many are wonderful catalysts.

prompt: When the metal in a phosphine complex is oxidized, the M–P bonds get longer and the P–R bonds get shorter. What does this show about backbonding to phosphines?

choices.text: The metal backbonds into P–R σ* orbitals; oxidation weakens backbonding, so less electron density sits in P–R antibonding orbitals
The metal backbonds into empty phosphorus 3d orbitals, which oxidation empties further
choices.why: The 3d orbitals are localized on phosphorus, so backbonding into them couldn't explain the change in P–R bond lengths.

choices.text: The metal backbonds into a phosphine π* orbital, as it does with CO
choices.why: Phosphines lack a π* orbital. Their backbonding is fundamentally different from CO's.

choices.text: Oxidation strengthens backbonding, which pulls the R groups closer to phosphorus
choices.why: Oxidation removes electron density from the metal, so it weakens backbonding. That is why the M–P bonds get longer.

explanation: Oxidation decreases the metal's ability to backbond, lowering the M–P bond order, so M–P bonds lengthen. The P–R bonds shorten because the acceptor orbitals have P–R antibonding character: phosphine backbonding is a dπ → σ*(P–R) interaction. Electron-withdrawing R groups and electron-rich metals help it.

prompt: Tolman ranked phosphines L by electron-donating ability using the C–O stretching frequency (ν_CO) of Ni(CO)3L complexes. As L becomes a stronger donor, how does ν_CO change?

choices.text: It decreases, because the more electron-rich Ni backbonds more into CO, lowering the C–O bond order
It increases, because a stronger donor raises the C–O bond order
choices.why: A stronger donor makes the metal more electron-rich, which increases backbonding into CO and lowers the C–O bond order.

choices.text: It increases, because stronger donors have wider cone angles
choices.why: Cone angle is Tolman's separate steric parameter. ν_CO tracks electronic effects, and it goes down for better donors.

choices.text: It doesn't change, because L doesn't affect the CO ligands
choices.why: L changes how electron-rich the Ni is, and that changes how much Ni backbonds into the CO ligands.

explanation: More strongly donating phosphines make the metal more electron-rich and better at CO backbonding. Better backbonding lowers the C–O bond order and so lowers ν_CO. Better donor ligands therefore have lower ν_CO values, and electron-withdrawing ligands higher ones. (Tolman's steric measure is the cone angle.)

prompt: Going from PMe3 to PH3 to PF3, the substituents become more electron-withdrawing. How do the ligands' σ-donor and π-acceptor properties change?

choices.text: The σ-donor properties weaken and the π-acceptor properties strengthen
The σ-donor properties strengthen and the π-acceptor properties weaken
choices.why: This is the reverse. Electron-withdrawing groups lower the HOMO, making the phosphine a weaker donor, and lower the LUMO, making it a better acceptor.

choices.text: Both the σ-donor and π-acceptor properties strengthen
choices.why: Lowering the HOMO and LUMO energies affects the two properties in opposite directions.

choices.text: Both the σ-donor and π-acceptor properties weaken
choices.why: The lower-energy LUMO, more localized on P, makes PF3 a better π-acceptor, not a worse one.

explanation: The HOMO and LUMO energies decrease from PMe3 to PH3 to PF3 as the substituent becomes more electron-withdrawing, so σ donation weakens and π acceptance strengthens. With strongly withdrawing groups the e-type LUMOs are also more localized on P, improving overlap with the metal. PF3 is a strong enough π-acceptor to form stable complexes with Pd and Pt in the 0 oxidation state, whose carbonyls are not known.

prompt: Why can PH3 act as a π-acceptor while NH3 cannot?

choices.text: PH3's LUMOs are low-lying antibonding 2e orbitals suited to π overlap
PH3 has an empty π* orbital, like CO
choices.why: Phosphines lack a π* orbital. PH3's π-acceptor orbitals are its antibonding 2e orbitals.

choices.text: PH3 accepts electron density into empty phosphorus 3d orbitals
choices.why: The section calls the 3d orbital explanation bogus. The acceptor orbitals are antibonding orbitals of the P–H (P–R) bonds.

choices.text: NH3's HOMO is higher in energy than PH3's, which stops it from accepting
choices.why: It is the other way around: PH3's HOMO is higher, which also makes PH3 the better σ-donor.

explanation: In NH3 the LUMO is the antibonding 3a1 orbital, while in PH3 the relative energies are swapped and the LUMOs are the antibonding 2e orbitals. These are relatively low-lying and have a suitable shape for π overlap with metal d orbitals. NH3's 2e orbitals are too high in energy for significant π-acceptor interactions. PH3's higher HOMO also makes it a better donor than NH3.

prompt: Mildly backbonding metals bind H2 side-on. Which two orbital interactions are involved?

choices.text: σ(H–H) → empty metal dσ, and filled metal dπ → σ*(H–H)
σ*(H–H) → empty metal dσ, and filled metal dπ → σ(H–H)
choices.why: This reverses the orbitals. The filled H–H σ orbital is the donor, and the empty σ* orbital is the acceptor.

choices.text: An H lone pair → empty metal dσ, with no back-donation
choices.why: H2 has no lone pair; it binds through the electrons of its σ bond. Back-donation into σ* is the second interaction.

choices.text: Filled metal dπ → an empty H2 π* orbital
choices.why: H2 has no π orbitals. The metal back-donates into the H–H σ* orbital.

explanation: Side-on H2 binding involves a σ interaction, σ(H–H) → dσ, and a π interaction, dπ → σ*(H–H). Strong back-donation into σ*(H–H) can cleave the H–H bond, so a dihydrogen complex can "tautomerize" to a dihydride isomer, an oxidative addition.

prompt: Binding H2 to a metal can lower its pKa by more than thirty units, while metal binding rarely changes the pKa of X–H ligands by more than 5. Why?

choices.text: The metal stabilizes the small, unhindered H^− conjugate base much more than larger, more electronegative anions like HO^− and NH2^−
H2 is already a strong acid before it binds, so a small change counts for more
choices.why: The section explains the huge pKa change by how well the metal stabilizes the conjugate base, H^−, not by the acidity of free H2.

choices.text: Back-donation into σ*(H–H) strengthens the H–H bond, which makes H^+ easier to lose
choices.why: Back-donation into σ* weakens the H–H bond. The key is stabilization of the conjugate base.

choices.text: X–H ligands bind through X, which keeps their protons from being removed
choices.why: X–H ligands can lose protons too; they are just acidified less, because the metal stabilizes HO^− or NH2^− much less than H^−.

explanation: The key is the conjugate base and how much the metal stabilizes it compared with the free anion. Metal stabilization of the unhindered H^− is much greater than that of larger, more electronegative anions like HO^− and NH2^−, so removing a proton from metal-bound H2 is especially favorable. σ complexes of electron-poor metals, especially cations, are stronger acids than related complexes of electron-rich metals.

prompt: For H2 bound to a metal, which kind of metal center most favors the dihydride (X2) form over the L-type σ complex?

choices.text: An electron-rich, π-basic metal center, which donates strongly into σ*(H–H)
An electron-poor, cationic metal center, which donates strongly into σ*(H–H)
choices.why: Electron-poor metals donate weakly into σ*(H–H). Their σ complexes are instead more acidic.

choices.text: A metal center with no d electrons, which accepts the H–H σ electrons most strongly
choices.why: Breaking the H–H bond to give the X2 isomer requires the metal to donate into σ*(H–H), which needs d electrons.

choices.text: Any metal from groups 6–9, since these always give dihydrides
choices.why: Groups 6–9 are where σ complexes are most common, because they balance π basicity and σ acidity.

explanation: More electron-rich metal centers favor the X2 isomer because they donate more strongly into σ*(H–H); Morris showed that H2 complexes of π-basic metal centers look like X2 complexes. σ complexes need a balance of π basicity and σ acidity (the "Goldilocks effect"), so they are most common for centrally located metals, groups 6–9.

prompt: How can a bridging hydride, associated with only two electrons, hold two metal centers together?

choices.text: Through three-center, two-electron bonding: it binds end-on to one metal, and that M–H σ bond binds side-on to the other
Each metal gets one of the hydride's two lone pairs
choices.why: A hydride is associated with only two electrons, one pair. Both metals share that pair in a three-center bond.

choices.text: It forms a linear M–H–M unit with two ordinary two-electron bonds
choices.why: Two ordinary bonds would need four electrons. Bridging hydride bond angles are never 180°, consistent with end-on plus side-on bonding.

choices.text: It acts as a Z-type ligand, accepting an electron pair from each metal
choices.why: The M–H σ bond acts as an electron donor to the second metal; the hydride doesn't accept electrons from the metals.

explanation: The M–H σ bond can itself act as an electron donor. A bridging hydride binds end-on to one metal like a standard X-type ligand and side-on to the other, like an L-type ligand but using σ electrons. This three-center, two-electron bonding explains why bridging hydride bond angles are never 180°.
